props.title: Summer Stock
props.initialSlug: Theater meets farm life in charming musical romp

sections.content: **Summer Stock** (1950) represents Gene Kelly and Judy Garland's final on-screen pairing, delivering a charming swan song to MGM's golden age musicals. The film's standout "Get Happy" number, with Garland in her iconic fedora and tuxedo jacket, became one of her signature performances despite being filmed months after principal photography wrapped. This production faced significant challenges - Garland struggled with personal issues and weight fluctuations throughout filming, yet managed to deliver powerhouse performances, particularly in "Friendly Star" and the newspaper dance with Kelly.

sections.content: The farm setting and "let's put on a show" plot connects directly to Garland's earlier Mickey & Rooney collaborations like **Babes in Arms** (1939) and **Strike Up the Band** (1940). Director Charles Walters, who previously worked with Garland on Easter Parade (1948), brings a light touch to the proceedings while still showcasing elaborate production numbers. Kelly's famous solo dance with a squeaky floorboard and newspaper demonstrates his genius for finding musicality in everyday objects, similar to his work in **Singin' in the Rain** (1952).

The film marks a transitional period in Hollywood musicals. While maintaining traditional elements like the backstage plot and romance-driven narrative seen in **The Barkleys of Broadway** (1949), it also hints at the more sophisticated direction the genre would take in films like **An American in Paris** (1951). Kelly's athletic choreography and Garland's powerful vocals bridge the gap between classical MGM style and emerging modern sensibilities. SUBHEAD: The End of an Era

sections.content: **Summer Stock** (1950) effectively closes the chapter on both Garland's MGM career and a certain style of musical filmmaking. Her next and final MGM film, **In the Good Old Summertime** (1949), had already been released when Summer Stock premiered. The production style - with its mix of elaborate soundstage numbers and intimate character moments - represents the last gasp of MGM's unit production system before the studio system's decline. This approach would soon give way to more realistic musicals like On the Town (1949) with its on-location shooting.
